title: The Ninth: Vienna, 1822–1824
subtitle: Commission, petition, premiere and aftermath of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony; Vienna and London, 1822–1825
intro: In November 1822 the Philharmonic Society of London offered Beethoven fifty pounds for a new symphony. He accepted, missed every deadline, and in February 1824 finished a work that ended, unprecedentedly, with soloists and chorus singing Schiller. That same month thirty Viennese patrons, publishers and musicians signed an address begging him not to give the premiere in Berlin. On 7 May 1824 the Ninth Symphony was first played at the court theatre by the Kärntnertor, with the composer on stage, unable to hear it.

This chapter is built from conversation books rather than diaries. Beethoven was almost totally deaf; visitors wrote their side of a conversation in pocket notebooks and he answered aloud, so the books preserve half of thousands of exchanges: his nephew Karl counting ticket sales, his secretary Anton Schindler grading the sopranos, Ignaz Schuppanzigh proposing a cheaper hall for the repeat. Around them sit dated letters, published reviews, the London minutes and journal, and a few late recollections.

The books are also a crime scene. Schindler, who kept them after Beethoven's death and sold them to Berlin in 1846, added well over a hundred fabricated entries to flatter himself and support his biography. Researchers identified the forgeries in the 1970s and the Berlin edition marks them. Every Schindler entry below states its status, and the most famous image of the night — Caroline Unger turning the deaf composer to see the applause — is given as what it is: a story she told George Grove in 1869, which later scholarship moves from the end of the symphony into the scherzo.

The record shows a night that was a triumph in the hall and a let-down at the box office. About 2,200 florins came in and only a few hundred remained. At a dinner two days later Beethoven accused his helpers of cheating him, and the repeat concert on 23 May, at midday in the Redoutensaal, drew a thin house. Within a year the symphony was heard in London in Italian, and in September 1825 the London conductor George Smart came to Baden to meet the composer.

Read across, the eyes split along a line of time. Karl, Schindler's genuine entries, Beethoven's own memoranda and the reviewers wrote within hours or days. Holz, Thalberg and Unger wrote or spoke years later, and Schindler's biography and forgeries came later still. The convergences show what each layer adds and what each may have invented.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian: both the Austrian Empire and Britain used the Gregorian calendar throughout. Many conversation-book entries are undated and are placed by their sequence in the books and by internal evidence, following the Berlin edition and Theodore Albrecht's chronology; recollections written later are shown on the day they describe, with the date of writing in the display date.

eyes.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
eyes.role: Composer, aged 51–54; almost totally deaf, conversing through notebooks in which visitors wrote and he answered aloud
eyes.side: Vienna; freelance composer with aristocratic patrons
eyes.where: Lodgings in Vienna (Ungargasse from autumn 1823); summers at Hetzendorf and Baden; on stage beside the conductor on 7 May 1824
eyes.vantage_label: the composer who could not hear his own premiere
eyes.form: dated letters, notes and his own conversation-book jottings
eyes.authenticity: Letters survive largely in autograph (many at the Beethoven-Haus Bonn and the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin); the conversation books (139 surviving) mostly record other people's side of conversations, with Beethoven's own memoranda and musical notes. Several 1824 notes are undated and dated only by context.
eyes.bio: By 1822 Beethoven had not given a public concert of new works for a decade. The London commission gave him a deadline for a symphony he had sketched on and off since 1818, and in 1823–24 he added a choral finale on Schiller's 'An die Freude'. His notes show a man managing copyists, censors, ticket prices and a nephew while finishing the work.

sources.title: Thayer's Life of Beethoven, vol. III (Krehbiel ed., Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Anton Felix Schindler
eyes.role: Unpaid secretary and factotum, aged 28–29; organised tickets, contracts and copyists for the 1824 concerts
eyes.where: Vienna, at Beethoven's side and at the theatre box office
eyes.vantage_label: the secretary at his elbow — and the later forger
eyes.form: conversation-book entries (some genuine, some forged after 1827) and a biography (1840)
eyes.authenticity: UNRELIABLE IN PART. Schindler took possession of the conversation books after Beethoven's death and sold them to the Royal Library in Berlin in 1846. He inserted fabricated entries after 1827 (counts range from about 120 to about 150), which were identified in the 1970s (Peter Stadlen; Dagmar Beck and Grita Herre at the 1977 Berlin Beethoven congress, published 1979) and are marked in the Berlin edition. Genuine entries in his hand are a key source; every Schindler entry here states its status.
eyes.bio: Schindler was the indispensable organiser of the 1824 concerts and their most self-serving narrator. His genuine notebook entries show the logistics hour by hour; his inserted entries and his 1840 biography enlarge his own role and colour the story of the premiere that most readers still know.

sources.title: Unheard Beethoven: 'Beethoven 200 years ago today' (Albrecht's conversation-book chronology)
Lockwood on the conversation books and Schindler's forgeries, New York Review of Books (2020)

eyes.name: Karl van Beethoven
eyes.role: The composer's nephew and ward, aged 17–18; university student who handled errands and money
eyes.where: Vienna; sat in the parterre (stalls) on 7 May 1824
eyes.authenticity: Karl's entries in the conversation books are in his own hand and generally regarded as genuine; they are datable by sequence and content (Berlin edition; Albrecht's English edition).
eyes.bio: Karl carried messages, counted ticket sales and collected the takings. He chose a seat in the stalls to hear well and to overhear opinions, which makes his notes the closest thing to an audience report from inside the family.

eyes.name: Ignaz Schuppanzigh
eyes.role: Violinist, aged 47–48; back in Vienna in 1823 after seven years in Russia; led (concertmaster) the orchestra at both 1824 concerts
eyes.authenticity: His entries survive in the conversation books (e.g. Book 67, May 1824); his playful third-person style is distinctive.
eyes.bio: Beethoven's oldest professional ally among the string players, mocked for his girth but trusted with the orchestra. His notebook entries at the 9 May dinner are practical: halls, prices, capacity for a second concert.

eyes.name: Count Moritz Lichnowsky
eyes.role: Aristocratic amateur and long-time Beethoven patron, aged 52–53
eyes.side: Viennese nobility; signatory of the February 1824 petition
eyes.form: signed petition; conversation-book entries; recipient of Beethoven's notes
eyes.authenticity: The petition survives (formerly Prussian State Library, Berlin); Beethoven's angry note to him of early April 1824 survives in autograph at the Beethoven-Haus (NE 67).
eyes.bio: Moritz Lichnowsky gathered signatures for the petition that kept the premiere in Vienna, and later intervened with the police president to get the Mass movements past the censor. He was also on the receiving end of Beethoven's rage when plans stalled.

sources.title: Beethoven to Moritz Lichnowsky, early April 1824 (Beethoven-Haus Bonn)

eyes.name: Carl Czerny
eyes.role: Pianist and teacher, aged 32–33; former Beethoven pupil; one of only three professional musicians among the petition's thirty signatories
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Friedrich Wieck of 9 May 1824 is cited in Albrecht's chronology; Beethoven's letter to him of 21 May 1824 survives in autograph (Beethoven-Haus, HCB BBr 12).
eyes.bio: Czerny heard the premiere as a professional who knew Beethoven's music from the inside. Within two weeks Beethoven asked him to play at the repeat concert, and he refused, judging himself unprepared.

eyes.name: Henriette Sontag
eyes.role: Soprano, aged 18; rising star of the Kärntnertortheater
eyes.authenticity: Her exchange with Beethoven in January 1824 is known from the conversation books as summarised by Thayer; the exact wording and hand should be checked against the Berlin edition.
eyes.bio: Sontag, still a teenager, had the soprano part in the Mass and the symphony. Schindler rated her far more accurate than her colleague; she had offered early on to help fill the house.

eyes.name: Caroline Unger
eyes.role: Contralto, aged 20; later an international opera star (Unger-Sabatier)
eyes.where: Soloists' row, Kärntnertortheater; recounted the premiere in London in 1869
eyes.form: oral account recorded by George Grove (1869)
eyes.authenticity: FLAGGED. The famous story that Unger turned Beethoven to see the applause has no 1824 eyewitness record. George Grove printed it, saying he had it from Madame Sabatier-Unger herself in London in 1869; it circulated earlier in other versions. Albrecht, using Karl Holz's later notebook account, places the moment during the scherzo rather than at the end.
eyes.bio: Unger sang the contralto solos at twenty and lived to tell the most quoted story of the night, forty-five years later. Her account is precious and late: a performer's memory, not a diary.

sources.title: Grove's footnote on the Unger anecdote (Wikisource mirror)

eyes.name: Friedrich August Kanne
eyes.role: Composer and critic, aged 45; editor of the Viennese Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung
eyes.where: In the audience at the Kärntnertortheater
eyes.authenticity: Review in Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung mit besonderer Rücksicht auf den österreichischen Kaiserstaat 8 (12 May 1824), p. 120; translated in the Boston University Beethoven Center critical-reception series.
eyes.bio: Kanne, a friend of Beethoven, wrote the first press notice within five days. He blamed the theatre, not the music, for half the effect being lost.

sources.title: Critical reception of Opp. 123–124 (Beethoven Center, San José / BU translations)

eyes.name: Sigismond Thalberg
eyes.role: Boy pianist, aged 12, in the audience; later a celebrated virtuoso
eyes.form: oral recollection recorded by A. W. Thayer (28 November 1860)
eyes.authenticity: Recollection given to Thayer 36 years after the event; Thayer used it in his biography. Treated here as a late memory.
eyes.bio: Thalberg's memory is a child's-eye view of the stage arrangements: who held the beat, who sat at the piano. It matters because it is independent of Schindler.

eyes.name: Karl Holz
eyes.role: Civil servant and violinist in Schuppanzigh's quartet from 1823; Beethoven's close aide from 1825
eyes.authenticity: Holz's description of the scherzo applause is in Conversation Book 114 (fol. 16r), written about two years after the premiere; genuine, but retrospective.
eyes.bio: Holz displaced Schindler as Beethoven's right hand in 1825. His notebook account of the applause breaking into the scherzo is the main written check on the later legends.

eyes.name: Ferdinand Ries
eyes.role: Pianist-composer, aged 38–41; Beethoven's former pupil and his agent in London until 1824
eyes.side: London Philharmonic Society; then the Rhineland
eyes.authenticity: Ries's letters are known through Beethoven's correspondence editions and Thayer; Beethoven's letters to him survive in autograph.
eyes.bio: Ries brokered the London commission and then, back in Germany, conducted one of the first performances outside Vienna and London. His letters measure the Ninth from far away.

eyes.name: Sir George Thomas Smart
eyes.role: Conductor and organist, aged 48–49; founding member of the Philharmonic Society
eyes.where: Argyll Rooms, London; Vienna and Baden in September 1825
eyes.vantage_label: the London conductor who came to see for himself
eyes.authenticity: Smart's travel journal was published as Leaves from the Journals of Sir George Smart (1907); his annotated programme for 21 March 1825 is in the British Library.
eyes.bio: Smart conducted the London premiere with a finale sung in Italian, then travelled to Vienna six months later partly to ask the composer how it should go. His journal is the coda's English-language eye.

entries.headline: Ries passes on London's offer of fifty pounds
entries.digest: Five days after the Philharmonic Society's directors voted to offer fifty pounds for a manuscript symphony, Ries wrote to Vienna with the terms. The Society wanted the score by the following March and exclusive use for eighteen months, after which Beethoven could sell it. For a cash-poor composer it was a deadline as much as a fee.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III, ch. on 1822 (resolution of 10 Nov 1822; Ries letter 15 Nov)

entries.headline: Accepting the London commission, with a sigh about money
entries.digest: Beethoven accepted the Society's offer. He told Ries that if he were not poor he would write for the first artists of Europe for nothing, a line that frames the whole story to come: the symphony was art, but also rent.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (letter to Ries, 20 Dec 1822)

entries.headline: Promising London a symphony 'soon'
entries.digest: Writing to Ries, Beethoven said the symphony would soon go to London by an embassy courier and complained that his brother Johann had offered a new overture to a London publisher behind his back. The symphony was nowhere near finished; the promise bought time.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (letter to Ries, 5 Feb 1823)

entries.headline: Back from Russia, the quartet resumes
entries.digest: After seven years away Schuppanzigh restarted his subscription quartet meetings, with the young Karl Holz on second violin. The players who would lead the 1824 orchestra and, later, premiere the late quartets were reassembling.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (Schuppanzigh's return 1823)

entries.headline: The symphony demands completion
entries.digest: In the summer lodgings at Hetzendorf the symphony became the main work. Through the autumn, back in town, Beethoven worked chiefly on the last movement; the third movement was complete in sketch before the fourth, and by the end of the year the whole work existed in sketches.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III, summer–autumn 1823

entries.headline: A teenage soprano offers to fill the house
entries.digest: When Beethoven doubted a concert could pay, the conversation books record Sontag asking when it would be and offering her help to guarantee a full house. It is an early sign that the singers wanted this premiere as much as the patrons did.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (conversation-book exchange, Jan 1824, as summarised)

entries.headline: The score is written out
entries.digest: By February the full score of the symphony was complete. At almost the same moment Beethoven had asked Count Brühl, intendant in Berlin, whether the new Mass and symphony could be given there, and Brühl was favourable. Vienna's music lovers heard rumours that the premiere might go north.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (completion Feb 1824; Brühl inquiry before Feb)

entries.headline: Thirty signatures to keep the premiere in Vienna
entries.digest: Count Moritz Lichnowsky was the most active collector of signatures for a florid address dated 'Vienna, in February 1824', begging Beethoven not to let his new works be heard first elsewhere. Most of the thirty signers were patrons, officials and publishers; the address is now linked to the Ludlamshöhle circle of writers.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III; Albrecht 2024, ch. 2

entries.headline: A pupil among the patrons
entries.digest: Czerny signed the petition, one of only three working musicians among the thirty names beside the abbé Stadler and Anton Halm. In late April he told Schindler he believed the official Stainer von Felsburg had drafted it.
entries.source_note: Albrecht 2024, ch. 2 abstract (signatories; Schindler's entry of 27 April)

entries.headline: A caller with an important message
entries.digest: Karl wrote that a visitor had called while his uncle was out, apparently bearing something important. Albrecht reads this as the first attempt to deliver the petition.
entries.source_note: Albrecht 2024, ch. 2 (conversation book, 25 Feb 1824)

entries.headline: Negotiating theatres and fees
entries.digest: Schindler reported that the concert would be in Vienna after all, and that Count Pálffy offered the Theater an der Wien for a fee recorded variously as 1,000 or 1,200 florins. Haggling over halls, orchestra size and the double-strength chorus filled March and April. Status: contemporary conversation-book material as used by Thayer; Schindler's own later narrative of these weeks is less reliable.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (consultation 2 March 1824 and following)

entries.headline: 'The concert will not take place'
entries.digest: Exasperated by delays, Beethoven sent short notes cancelling everything and telling friends not to visit; the one to Count Moritz Lichnowsky survives in his own hand. He suspected his helpers of intrigue and made their work twice as hard.
entries.source_note: Autograph note to M. Lichnowsky, early April 1824, Beethoven-Haus Bonn NE 67

entries.headline: Talking the Mass past the censor
entries.digest: Church music could not be sung in a theatre, and Beethoven's own appeal to the censor failed. Lichnowsky took the matter to Police President Sedlnitzky, and the three Mass movements were allowed on the bill as 'hymns'.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (April 1824)

entries.headline: Switching to the Kärntnertor and Duport
entries.digest: After the concert had been announced on 21 April for the Theater an der Wien, the plan moved to the court theatre at the Kärntnertor, whose administrator Louis Duport agreed terms. In his later account Schindler dated Beethoven's request to Duport to 24 April and put the hall fee at 400 florins; the contract he says he closed himself.
entries.source_note: Kalischer letters vol. 2, footnote to no. 370 (Schindler's statement); Thayer vol. III

entries.headline: Final rehearsal: the soprano is 'ten times' surer
entries.digest: Schindler collected Beethoven and Karl at about half past eight and picked up the two soloists on the way. He judged Umlauf still unsure of the score and tiring, and Sontag far more accurate than Unger. Status: these entries are treated as genuine; the remainder of Conversation Book 65 is filled with Schindler's forged entries, including chatter about Beethoven's green coat.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 65, via Albrecht, Unheard Beethoven 6 May 1824

entries.headline: Nobody will understand the words
entries.digest: Karl and Schindler agreed that the chorus's German would be unintelligible from the seats, so the text of Schiller's ode should be printed for the audience. Five hundred copies were ordered.
entries.source_note: Albrecht, Unheard Beethoven 6 May 1824

entries.headline: Last-minute notes in his own hand
entries.digest: In the notebook Beethoven jotted revisions on the eve of the premiere: the contrabassoon, a possible variant for the bass soloist, a note for Unger in the Credo, a b-natural for the tenor in the Dona nobis. He planned to go through the whole score with Umlauf.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 65, fols. 34r–41r, via Unheard Beethoven 6 May 1824

entries.headline: Boxes sold, the gallery full
entries.digest: At midday Karl reported that the boxes were gone, some sold at premiums of 25 and 50 florins, and the fourth gallery was sold out. The imperial box would be empty: the Emperor had left Vienna two days earlier.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 66, via Unheard Beethoven 7 May 1824

entries.headline: Beating time to music he could not hear
entries.digest: At seven the concert began: the Consecration of the House overture, the Kyrie, Credo and Agnus Dei, then the new symphony. Umlauf conducted and Schuppanzigh led, while Beethoven stood beside the conductor giving the tempos and following his score. It ended around half past nine.
entries.source_note: Leipzig AMZ 26 (1 July 1824), cols. 437–42; Unheard Beethoven 7 May 1824

entries.headline: A boy notices who really held the beat
entries.digest: Thalberg, twelve at the time, later told Thayer that Umlauf had warned singers and players to keep their eyes on his beat rather than the composer's, and that Conradin Kreutzer sat at the piano. It is a calm, practical memory that bypasses Schindler entirely.
entries.source_note: Thayer's notes of 28 Nov 1860, cited in Unheard Beethoven 7 May 1824

entries.headline: Applause breaks into the scherzo
entries.digest: Writing in a conversation book about two years later, Holz told Beethoven that the audience had burst into applause during the scherzo, interrupting the music. Albrecht uses this to place the moment when the deaf composer had to be shown the applause within the symphony, not at its end.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 114, fol. 16r, via Unheard Beethoven 7 May 1824

entries.headline: Turning him to face the house — a late story
entries.digest: In London in 1869 Madame Sabatier-Unger told George Grove that Beethoven, still facing the orchestra, was unaware of the applause until she turned him round to see it. No 1824 source records this; the story had already circulated in several forms, and the timing (end of the symphony, or mid-scherzo) is disputed.
entries.source_note: Grove, footnote in his study of the Ninth; Albrecht's redating via Holz

entries.headline: 'Never such stormy applause' — possibly forged
entries.digest: An entry in Schindler's hand says he had never in his life heard applause so stormy and sincere. Its status is uncertain: it may be one of his later insertions. His 1840 biography's story of Beethoven fainting after the concert conflicts with the genuine notebook record.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 66 (status flagged by Albrecht); Thayer vol. III on the fainting story

entries.headline: The singers hardly applauded
entries.digest: Karl reported that Sontag and Unger got little applause because the public felt it should cheer only Beethoven at his own concert. He listed who had bought seats — the violinist Mayseder took six, Count Lichnowsky came, a cloth merchant paid double — and said he had sat in the stalls to hear well and hear opinions.
entries.source_note: Conversation books, via Unheard Beethoven 8 May 1824

entries.headline: London would pay ten times as much
entries.digest: Schindler set the box-office settlement for five o'clock at the theatre. Later he told Beethoven he could earn 12,000 to 15,000 florins in London or Paris against 1,200 to 1,500 in Vienna, and bristled at Johann van Beethoven's threat to push him out of the house. Status: these entries are treated as genuine.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 66, via Unheard Beethoven 8 May 1824

entries.headline: Paying the cleaners, buying seltzer water
entries.digest: Beethoven's own memoranda on the day after his triumph are domestic: pay the theatre cleaners, see the lawyer Bach, buy seltzer water, settle the maid's wages. The takings that evening were a shock: about 2,200 florins gross, with only a few hundred left once hall, performers and the 700-florin copying bill were paid.
entries.source_note: Unheard Beethoven 8 May 1824; Thayer vol. III (2,200 gross, about 420 remaining); Leipzig AMZ (net 300 fl. W.W.)

entries.headline: Planning a second concert over dinner
entries.digest: At the restaurant in the Prater Schuppanzigh proposed a repeat on 14 May in the Landständischer Saal, free of hall rent, with a smaller orchestra, tickets at three or four florins and room for perhaps 800. When Beethoven would not be reasoned with, he too left the table.
entries.source_note: Conversation Book 67, via Unheard Beethoven 9 May 1824

entries.headline: The dinner row: accused of cheating
entries.digest: Beethoven accused the theatre management and Schindler of cheating him over the takings. Umlauf and Schuppanzigh said the accounts had passed two cashiers and tallied; Schindler and Umlauf walked out, and the guests finished their meal elsewhere. Schindler later dated the row to after the second concert, and his post-mortem addendum in Book 67 (fol. 10v) is judged highly unreliable; the genuine sequence places it on 9 May.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (dinner); Albrecht, Unheard Beethoven 9 May 1824 (dating and addendum)

entries.headline: Leaving early to study
entries.digest: Fetched from his boarding house for the dinner, Karl ate quickly and left to study before the quarrel broke out in earnest.
entries.source_note: Unheard Beethoven 9 May 1824

entries.headline: Reporting the premiere to Leipzig
entries.digest: Czerny wrote to the Leipzig piano teacher Friedrich Wieck about the concert, describing how applause had interrupted the scherzo. It is the earliest outside report from a trained musician.
entries.source_note: Albrecht's chronology, Unheard Beethoven 7 May 1824 (letter cited, text not consulted)

entries.headline: A packed house, half the sound lost
entries.digest: Kanne's review described an extraordinarily large audience but argued that the sacred movements belonged in another kind of hall, that chorus and soloists were under-rehearsed, and that the open stage scattered the sound. The overture and symphony struck harder; he praised Umlauf and hoped for a second performance in a better room.
entries.source_note: Wiener AMZ 8 (12 May 1824), p. 120 (BU/Beethoven Center translation)

entries.headline: Asking Czerny to replace the Mass
entries.digest: Unhappy with the chorus, Beethoven wrote asking Czerny to play two movements of the 'Emperor' Concerto at the repeat concert in place of parts of the Missa solemnis.
entries.source_note: Autograph letter, Beethoven-Haus Bonn HCB BBr 12

entries.headline: Declining to play
entries.digest: Czerny turned the request down, feeling insufficiently prepared at a day or two's notice. The programme was patched instead with an Italian aria and an old trio announced as new.
entries.source_note: Beethoven-Haus note on HCB BBr 12; Thayer vol. III (programme of 23 May)

entries.headline: A half-empty hall on a fine Sunday
entries.digest: The repeat was held at midday in the large Redoutensaal. Only the Kyrie survived from the Mass; Beethoven's trio 'Tremate' was billed as new though more than twenty years old. Attendance was poor and the concert ran about 800 florins short; Duport's guaranteed 500 florins, which Beethoven had been talked into accepting, was all he got.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III; Wiener Zeitschrift 3 June 1824

entries.headline: The London premiere, finale in Italian
entries.digest: Smart conducted the Philharmonic Society's first performance, with Franz Cramer leading and Caradori, Goodall, Vaughan and Phillips as soloists; the choral finale was sung in an Italian translation. A first half of Haydn, Mozart, Handel, Reicha and Cherubini preceded it. Smart's annotated programme survives in the British Library.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, British premiere of the Ninth; Beethoven-Haus 'Beethoven and Great Britain'

entries.headline: Corrections for the Rhineland
entries.digest: Writing to Ries, now in Germany, Beethoven sent corrections to the score and parts — down to a wrong note in the first oboe — for a performance at the Lower Rhine festival in Aachen.
entries.source_note: Kalischer letters vol. 2, no. 403

entries.headline: Precision in Aachen
entries.digest: Ries reported that the symphony had been played at the Aachen festival with remarkable precision, the finale alone rehearsed for three hours, and sent Beethoven a fee of forty louis d'or.
entries.source_note: Kalischer letters vol. 2, footnote to no. 426 (Ries to Beethoven, 9 June 1825)

entries.headline: Meeting the composer at a quartet rehearsal
entries.digest: Smart heard a new Beethoven quartet played privately in the rooms of the publisher Schlesinger and met the composer, who now had Holz at his side in place of Schindler. Smart came partly to learn how the Ninth was meant to go.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (Smart in Vienna, 7–20 Sept 1825); Complete Beethoven chronology

entries.headline: A diamond pin and a two-minute canon
entries.digest: On his last visit, at Baden, Smart gave Beethoven a diamond pin. In return Beethoven wrote out the little canon 'Ars longa, vita brevis' for him, dated that day; Smart's journal notes it took about two minutes.
entries.source_note: Beethoven-Haus Bonn on WoO 192 and Smart's diary; Thayer vol. III

entries.headline: The biography that fixed the legend
entries.digest: Schindler published his Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven, casting himself as the composer's indispensable friend. Its dramatic account of the 1824 concerts, including Beethoven collapsing afterwards, conflicts with the conversation books he controlled — the same books into which he had inserted entries.
entries.source_note: Thayer vol. III (critique of Schindler); NYRB 2020

claims.evidence: Society directors' resolution as cited by Thayer vol. III

claims.evidence: Sketch chronology in Thayer vol. III

Thirty Viennese sign the petition asking for the premiere in Vienna, not Berlin or London
claims.evidence: Petition (formerly Prussian State Library); Albrecht 2024 ch. 2

claims.claim: Copy of the score handed to the Philharmonic's agent in Vienna for London

claims.evidence: Concert poster; Leipzig AMZ 1 July 1824; conversation books

claims.evidence: Grove's footnote; Holz, Conversation Book 114; Albrecht

Wiener Zeitschrift (critic '*—*') says expectations were surpassed

convergences.label: The petition month
convergences.note: The score is finished, a Berlin performance is in the air, patrons collect signatures, and Karl logs a mysterious caller. The same month reads as triumph to the signers and as pressure to the composer.

convergences.label: Final rehearsal in the Redoutensaal
convergences.note: Schindler grades the singers, Karl worries about the words, Beethoven writes notes for the contrabassoon — and the same notebook is later padded with Schindler's forgeries.

convergences.label: The premiere, Kärntnertortheater
convergences.note: Box-office bustle at noon, the composer beating time, a boy watching the conductor, a violinist remembering applause in the scherzo, a singer's story forty-five years on, and a secretary's possibly forged superlative: one evening, six layers of reliability.

convergences.label: Counting the money
convergences.note: Karl reports who paid what; Schindler dreams of London fees; Beethoven buys seltzer water and learns how little is left.

convergences.label: Dinner at Zum wilden Mann
convergences.note: Plans for a second concert turn into an accusation of cheating, while across town Czerny writes the premiere up for Leipzig. Schindler's later redating of the row is contradicted by the books.

convergences.label: Patching the repeat
convergences.note: Beethoven tries to replace the Mass with a concerto; Czerny declines; on 23 May the hall is half empty.

convergences.label: The Ninth leaves Vienna
convergences.note: London hears it in Italian; Beethoven sends Ries corrections for Aachen; Ries reports precision. The work's reception abroad begins within a year.

convergences.label: Smart at Baden
convergences.note: The London conductor finally meets the composer: a pin, a canon, and Holz where Schindler used to stand.

ties.note: Secretary and employer; Schindler's genuine entries and his later forgeries both sit in Beethoven's notebooks.
Uncle and ward; Karl ran errands and money for the concerts.
Worked together on the concerts while Karl relayed Johann's wish to be rid of Schindler.
Old friends; Schuppanzigh led the orchestra and walked out of the 9 May dinner.
Patron and petitioner, and recipient of Beethoven's furious April note.
Fellow signatories of the February 1824 petition.
Former teacher and pupil; Beethoven's letter of 21 May 1824 asked Czerny to play.
The two young soloists rehearsed and sang side by side; Schindler compared them unfavourably to each other.
She sang his contralto solos and later told the story of turning him to the audience.
Second violin in Schuppanzigh's quartet from 1823.
Holz replaced Schindler as Beethoven's aide in 1825; Schindler later belittled him.
Former pupil turned London agent; letters carried the commission and the corrections.
Colleagues in the Philharmonic Society that commissioned the symphony.
Met in Vienna and Baden in September 1825; Beethoven wrote him a canon.

threads_out.note: In 1902 the Vienna Secession built an exhibition around Max Klinger's Beethoven statue, with Klimt's Beethoven Frieze interpreting the Ninth's finale and Mahler conducting an arrangement from it at the opening.
At Christmas 1989 Leonard Bernstein conducted the Ninth in East and West Berlin after the Wall opened, substituting 'Freiheit' for 'Freude' in Schiller's text.

The Ninth was performed for Nazi state occasions, including Furtwängler's 1942 concert on the eve of Hitler's birthday, while it was also played in camps and exile; the same score served opposite meanings.
The Kärntnertortheater took its name from the Carinthian Gate in the city walls that had held against the Ottoman siege of 1683; those fortifications still ringed the inner city in 1824.
